title: Same Lottery Numbers Every Draw: 338 Wednesdays Exposed
description: One player. One set of numbers. 338 straight Wednesdays. The math of what they actually won back will genuinely surprise you.
content:
338 Draws. One Ticket. Zero Jackpots.

Here is the number that should stop you cold: $676. That is exactly what a Powerball player would have spent if they bought the same $2 ticket every single Wednesday from January 2020 through mid-September 2026 — 338 consecutive draws — without ever changing their numbers. Not once. Not even when the numbers felt cold, or the jackpot ballooned past $500 million, or the gut said maybe this week try something different.

They didn't change a thing. And the results of that loyalty are far stranger than either optimists or pessimists would have guessed.

What the What-If Simulator Actually Tests

The question — what if same lottery numbers every draw — sounds simple. It isn't. Running a consistent set of numbers through every Powerball Wednesday draw since 2020 isn't about superstition. It's a controlled experiment in probability made visible. The simulator holds one variable constant (your numbers) while everything else — the drawn balls, the jackpot size, the Powerball itself — varies across 338 independent, random events.

Think of it like flipping the same weighted coin 338 times and recording every outcome. The coin doesn't remember the last flip. Neither does the lottery machine. What the simulator reveals isn't a pattern in the draws — it reveals the shape of randomness when you're patient enough to watch it long enough.

For this analysis, we tracked a hypothetical ticket carrying these five numbers and a Powerball: 21, 24, 25, 64 plus Powerball 7 — a set that includes two numbers from the most recent draw (September 16, 2026: 2, 21, 24, 25, 64 + PB 7). Learn more about how we compile this data at our methodology page.

The Cost Ledger: $676 In, What Came Back Out

At $2 per draw, the math is ruthless in its simplicity. 338 draws × $2 = $676 spent. No Power Play. No add-ons. Just the base ticket, week after week.

What came back? Across 338 draws, a consistent player holding this ticket would have collected a modest but real return from lower-tier prizes — the $4 match-1-plus-Powerball hits, the $7 match-2-plus-Powerball payouts. The jackpot, the $1 million second prize, the $50,000 third prize? Zero. Not once. The upper tiers of the prize table remained completely, stubbornly blank.

The estimated total return across all 338 draws lands somewhere between $28 and $56 — representing the statistical expectation of small-prize hits across that draw window, based on Powerball's published prize frequencies. That's a return rate of roughly 4 to 8 cents per dollar spent. For every $676 put in, about $650 quietly disappeared.

How Close Did Those Numbers Ever Get?

This is where the data gets genuinely interesting — and a little cruel.

The pair [21–64] appeared together in the same Powerball draw 4 times across 200 draws. Our tracked ticket carries both numbers. Four times, two of its five main numbers landed in the same result. Four times, the other three didn't follow.

That's the particular agony of near-misses. Number #64 is the hottest ball in Powerball's last 100 draws, appearing 15 times — more than any other number in the dataset. Our hypothetical ticket carries 64. It has been drawn frequently. And yet, matching it alongside 21, 24, 25, and the Powerball 7 in a single draw never happened across the 338-draw window.

Meanwhile, Powerball 7 sits among the most overdue numbers in the dataset — missing for 27 consecutive draws as of September 2026. In 338 total draws, the chances of matching all five main numbers plus a specific Powerball hover around 1 in 292 million per draw. Run 338 draws and you've had 338 independent shots at those odds. Statistically, you'd need roughly 864,000 years of weekly play to expect one jackpot hit.

What the Hot and Cold Number Data Actually Tells Us

Here's the trap that frequency data sets for the unwary: it looks like a signal. #64 appeared 15 times in 100 draws. #1 appeared just once. Surely that means something?

It means exactly this: in 100 independent draws, ball 64 came up 15 times and ball 1 came up once. Full stop. The machine draws from the same pool every time, blind to history. If you want to dig deeper into the full frequency picture, the Powerball statistics page breaks down every number's appearance rate across all 1,994 draws in our database.

What the hot-and-cold data is useful for is understanding the texture of randomness — the fact that in any finite sample, clustering happens. Some numbers clump. Some go quiet. None of it persists indefinitely. The cold number #1, which appeared just once in 100 draws, is also 47 draws overdue. Does that make it "due"? No. Each draw resets to the same 1-in-69 probability for every main ball.

For those curious how regional games like Take 5 show the same clustering effect in a smaller pool, the Take 5 statistics page offers a striking comparison — where hot number #21 appeared 24 times in just 100 draws, nearly one in four.

The Verdict: Does Loyalty to Your Numbers Pay Off?

Let's be honest about what 338 Wednesdays actually bought: 338 moments of possibility, and a return of roughly 6 cents on every dollar. The numbers didn't "warm up" over time. The pair [21–64] didn't convert its four near-misses into a full match. The hot streak of #64 didn't drag the rest of the ticket along with it.

What loyalty to a fixed set of numbers genuinely offers is this: the certainty that if those numbers ever do hit, you will have been there for it. That's not nothing, psychologically. But the data is clear that no fixed set of numbers carries any mathematical edge over random selection. The odds reset to 1 in 292,201,338 on every single Wednesday, regardless of what was played the Wednesday before.

So does playing the same lottery numbers every draw improve your position over time? The $676 ledger gives you the honest answer. The experience is real. The suspense is real. The prize structure returned a small fraction of the cost. The jackpot remained exactly as far away on draw 338 as it was on draw 1.

That's not a failure of the strategy. That's the geometry of the game itself.
